Gujarat's role in scientific development

National science policy establishes broad priorities for India, while state governments can develop policies and institutions suited to regional needs. Gujarat has important activities in space science, industrial research, biotechnology, agricultural research, plasma science and scientific education.

The distinction between geographical location and administrative control is important. An institution can be situated in Gujarat while belonging to a central government department or a national research network.

Gujarat Council on Science and Technology

The Gujarat Council on Science and Technology (GUJCOST) is a state-level body functioning under the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology. It was established in September 1986 as a State Science and Technology Council and subsequently developed its autonomous institutional structure.

GUJCOST promotes scientific awareness, education, research-related activities and the development of science and technology in Gujarat. It provides an important link between state policy priorities and scientific institutions, students and the wider public.

Gujarat Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2026–2031

The Government of Gujarat launched the Gujarat STI Policy 2026–2031 in March 2026. Unlike the national draft STIP 2020, this is a state policy issued for the specified policy period. The Gujarat Department of Science and Technology identifies GUJCOST as the implementing organisation.

The policy seeks to strengthen research and innovation in areas such as biotechnology, semiconductors, artificial intelligence, green energy, defence and space technologies. It also emphasises research infrastructure, skilled scientific personnel, intellectual-property development and cooperation between academic institutions and industry.

Major policy provisions and targets

  • Research funding: A proposed dedicated fund of Rs 1,000 crore to support research and indigenous technological development. The detailed policy document identifies the Swadeshi Anusandhan Fund.
  • Research workforce: A target of developing 1 lakh highly skilled research professionals by 2031.
  • Research expenditure: An ambition to increase the state's R&D expenditure to 1% of Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP).
  • Intellectual property: A target of more than 1,000 IP filings annually, including more than 500 patent filings.
  • Regional research collaboration: Proposed Gujarat Rajya Research and Innovation Clusters (GRRIC), beginning in the Gandhinagar–Ahmedabad region.

These numerical statements are policy commitments and targets stated for the 2026–2031 period. They should not be presented as expenditure already incurred, scientists already trained or patents already filed.

National and state policy targets use different economic denominators. The STI Policy 2013 stated a national GERD goal of 2% of India's GDP. The Gujarat STI Policy 2026–2031 sets a state R&D expenditure goal of 1% of Gujarat's GSDP. The two percentages concern different geographical economies and policy periods.

Several of these institutions belong to national departments or research councils. By contrast, GUJCOST and GBRC operate within Gujarat's state science and technology framework.

Understanding India's scientific institutions as a system

India's scientific institutions are best understood by identifying the particular problem each one addresses.

  • Research funding and coordination: ANRF and relevant science departments support the wider research system.
  • Basic and industrial science: TIFR, IISc and CSIR institutions create scientific knowledge and technologies.
  • Space: ISRO develops space technologies; IN-SPACe facilitates non-governmental activities; NSIL handles commercial responsibilities.
  • Defence: DRDO develops technologies relevant to national security.
  • Atomic energy: BARC undertakes research, NPCIL operates power reactors and AERB regulates nuclear and radiation safety.
  • Health and biotechnology: ICMR promotes biomedical research, while DBT supports biotechnology across sectors.
  • Agriculture: ICAR coordinates research and education, while KVKs help communicate and assess technologies at the field level.

These mandates can overlap in practice. A scientific technology may have applications in health, agriculture and industry, and several institutions may cooperate in developing it. The correct classification depends on the organisation's principal responsibility, not merely on the scientific subject it sometimes studies.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat STI Policy: 2026–2031; launched March 2026.
  • GUJCOST: state science and technology council and implementing organisation for the Gujarat STI Policy.
  • Gujarat policy research-fund provision: Rs 1,000 crore.
  • Gujarat policy R&D target: 1% of GSDP.
  • Gujarat policy skilled-researcher target: 1 lakh by 2031.
  • National STI Policy 2013: GERD goal of 2% of GDP.
  • Trap: Gujarat's operative 2026–2031 state policy must not be confused with the draft national STIP 2020.

[Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Gujarat Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2026–2031, Overview and Strategic Framework, including Swadeshi Anusandhan Fund; Government of Gujarat, DST, Gujarat Council on Science and Technology, Overview; Government of India, Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013, section Investment in Research and Development; Press Information Bureau, Implementation of National Science, Technology and Innovation Policy-2020, 29 January 2026; official institutional profiles of ISRO, PRL, CSIR-CSMCRI, IPR, GBRC, ICMR, ICAR and NPCIL; policy and institutional information reviewed against the content cutoff of 2 November 2026.]
